Summary

The same reward-locked signal reappears in the older cohort

This is the second of two independent cohorts run through the identical pipeline: same MATLAB-verified alignment and dF/F/z-score computation, same per-session hemisphere resolution, same two pooled GLMs, same four pre-specified within-animal RPE analyses. FP2's 4 mice are older animals than FP1's 7 — a separate question (addressed later, once both cohorts are in hand) is whether age changes anything about this encoding. On its own, FP2 reproduces FP1's core finding: reward delivery drives a large, sharply-timed change in the mPFC signal at side-port entry, and every mouse individually shows the same outcome×value interaction found in FP1.

Headline result. The pooled FIR model's out-of-sample R² (0.212 ± 0.015) lands within a hair of FP1's (0.176 ± 0.007) despite a completely disjoint set of animals and sessions. All 4 FP2 mice individually show a significant negative outcome×Q(chosen) interaction post-event, and none show it pre-event — the same clean temporal dissociation as FP1.

Data & validation

What went into this analysis

All 26 “none”-condition sessions from WCL30–33 were processed with the same MATLAB-verified pipeline used for FP1, with per-session hemisphere resolved from the RA's channel-detection scan (this cohort is almost entirely green_l, with one exception — WCL31's 08/01/23 session on green_r). Every session cleared QC with 0 skipped sessions in every batch step (condition batch, encoding GLM, FIR GLM, RPE data prep).

Model 1 — Time-resolved encoding GLM

A regression at every timepoint around side-port entry

Identical specification to the FP1 report: an independent OLS regression fit at each sample around side-port entry, predicting the trial-level z-scored signal from choice, reward, reward history, decision-value strength, and behavioral state. Numeric predictors were standardized, so each β is in units of signal change per 1 SD of that predictor.

Z ~ Choice * Reward + Reward_lag1 + Reward_lag2 + Reward_lag3 + Q_diff_abs + C(Behavioral_State)

Reading the panels

  • Reward — the same sharp step at t=0 seen in FP1, in the same direction, holding through the post-event window.
  • Model fit — low and flat before the event, rising sharply after t=0 as in FP1, consistent with an evoked rather than anticipatory response.
  • Reward_lag1–3 — the same smooth, event-independent history ramps as FP1, with no discontinuity at t=0.
  • Behavioral_State terms — clear post-event deviations from Exploitation, as in FP1.
Model 2 — FIR deconvolution GLM

Deconvolving the continuous trace directly

Identical specification to FP1: the full continuous z-scored trace regressed against time-shifted impulse regressors anchored at side-port entry, one 39-bin (±1.0 s) kernel per 3-trial reward-history pattern (reward_seq_3), plus parametric modulation by |Q difference| and choice side. Regularization chosen by RidgeCV; out-of-sample performance assessed with 10-fold GroupShuffleSplit cross-validation grouped by trial.

Reading the panels

  • Ordering by history — the same clean separation by recent-outcome baseline seen in FP1: recent-loss patterns sit high, recent-win patterns sit low, all sharing one underlying shape offset by history.
  • Shared shape — the same pre-event dip / post-event rebound-and-decay profile as FP1.

Within-animal analyses

The pre-specified confirmatory tests, at the animal level

The same four pre-specified analyses from the FP1 report, run separately within each of the 4 FP2 mice using trial-level model RPE derived from each animal's own sticky-Q fit (RPE_signed = outcome − Q(chosen action)). With only 4 animals, a Wilcoxon signed-rank test cannot reach conventional significance even with a unanimous result — the smallest possible two-sided p-value at n=4 is 0.125 (vs. 0.016 at FP1's n=7). Group-level tests are reported as run, but the more informative evidence here is the individual per-mouse results themselves.

1. Within-animal RPE regression

Post-event amplitude (mean z-score, 0–1 s after side-port entry) regressed on RPE_signed alone, separately per mouse.

All 4/4 mice show a significant negative βRPE (range −0.78 to −2.38, individually p from 7.4×10−7 to 1.6×10−138); Wilcoxon across the 4 mice hits the n=4 floor (p=0.125, W=0) — not significant by the conventional threshold, but that is a sample-size ceiling, not a weak effect: every single animal individually clears a far stricter bar. As in FP1, the single-predictor RPE model explains modest variance (R²=0.022–0.228) and in 3/4 mice explains less than outcome alone (WCL30 is the exception, where RPE outperforms outcome alone: 0.228 vs. 0.133). Letting outcome and value load freely (outcome × Q(chosen) interaction) again shows a negative, significant interaction in 4/4 mice (p from 0.035 to 1.8×10−18) — the same uniformly clean result as FP1.

2. Temporal specificity: does the value modulation appear before the event too?

The same interaction refit with pre_amp (mean z-score, −1 to 0 s before side-port entry) as the outcome, per mouse.

It vanishes just as cleanly as in FP1. Post-event: significant in 4/4 mice, uniformly negative. Pre-event: significant in 0/4 mice (p from 0.088 to 0.941), sign inconsistent across animals (2 negative, 2 positive, all near zero). The same within-animal temporal control that supported an outcome-locked interpretation in FP1 replicates exactly in this independent cohort.

3. Signed vs. unsigned RPE

5-fold cross-validated out-of-sample R², per mouse, comparing post_amp ~ RPE_signed + Q_diff_abs + choice_side against the same model with RPE_signed replaced by |RPE|.

Same non-confirmatory result as FP1. 3/4 mice show signed beating unsigned (ΔR² up to +0.222 in WCL30), 1/4 does not (WCL31, −0.016); Wilcoxon p=0.25, not significant. This mirrors FP1's own non-significant result on this specific test (4/7, p=0.22) — across both independent cohorts, this head-to-head comparison has not established that sign information reliably beats magnitude-only encoding at the group level.

4. Between-animal variability of the two pooled models

Both GLMs refit separately per mouse, from the same extracted data (no raw reprocessing) — encoding-model peak R² and FIR out-of-sample R², one point per animal.

Notably tighter than FP1: FIR out-of-sample R² ranges only 0.199–0.234 across all 4 mice (vs. FP1's 0.048–0.292) — every FP2 mouse has 5–8 sessions, with none of FP1's 2-session outliers dragging the spread down. Encoding-model peak R² is more variable (0.218–0.459), with WCL30 the standout — also the mouse with the strongest RPE regression result above (Analysis 1). One oddity worth flagging rather than over-interpreting: WCL31's peak R² timing lands later (~2.6 s post-event) than the other three mice (~0.9–1.2 s) — consistent with WCL31 also being the one mouse where signed RPE underperformed unsigned (Analysis 3) and outcome-only beat the full RPE model (Analysis 1). It is the same animal underperforming across independent analyses, which argues against pure sampling noise and for something specific to that mouse's data or fit — worth a closer look before pooling.

Interpretation

An independent replication, with an open question about one animal

FP2 was analyzed with a pipeline already fixed and verified against FP1, applied here without cohort-specific tuning. The core finding replicates cleanly: a reward-locked signal (both pooled models), value-dependent modulation of that response in the same direction in every one of the 4 mice, and a temporal control confirming that modulation is specific to the post-outcome window in every mouse and absent beforehand. The one test that did not confirm in FP1 (signed vs. unsigned RPE) also did not confirm here, at a similar effect size and in the same direction — a second independent instance of the same negative result strengthens rather than weakens the case that this specific comparison genuinely doesn't favor signed encoding in this data, rather than being an FP1-specific fluke.

The one thing that stands out as FP2-specific: WCL31 underperforms the other three mice on three unrelated analyses at once (weakest FIR-adjacent metrics, RPE model losing to outcome-only, signed RPE losing to unsigned, and a late-shifted encoding-GLM peak). That consistency across independent analyses is worth a closer look at that mouse's sessions specifically (e.g. its viral expression, session count and dates, or task engagement) before including it uncritically in the pooled cross-cohort comparison.

Scope. n=4 mice means the group-level Wilcoxon tests in this report cannot reach significance even under a unanimous individual result (floor p=0.125) — the individual per-mouse p-values are the stronger evidence here, not the group test. This covers only the “none” condition. Per the plan discussed, this FP2 result is a precursor to (1) a pooled analysis across all FP1+FP2 mice to check consistency of RPE encoding across the full dataset, and (2) a dedicated age-comparison analysis (FP2 vs. FP1) once both cohorts are finalized — with roughly a dozen more mice expected to be added to this cohort over time.
